I’m reading this as: a ring of LEN n is an n-sided shape with one bit on each flat face, and you enter it at one of its faces. Checking what that forces.

Count ring shapes, entry faces, and nesting
I took “LEN is the total flat surfaces” literally. A ring of LEN n is an n-sided shape with one bit on each face, and you enter it at one face. That makes every word on the ring two things: the shape, and the face you came in on. So the 2^n transformations on a ring aren’t 2^n separate things. They split into a few shapes, each entered at its faces.

LEN	words	shapes	new shapes × entry faces	shapes carried from smaller rings
1	2	2	2 × 1	—
2	4	3	1 × 2	2, from ring 1
4	16	6	3 × 4	3, from rings 1, 2
8	256	36	30 × 8 = 240	6, from rings 1, 2, 4
8 contains 4 contains 2 contains 1, exactly. No arranging by hand was needed:

The repeating shapes on ring 8 are exactly ring 4’s six shapes wrapped around twice.
Ring 4’s repeating shapes are ring 2’s three shapes wrapped twice.
Ring 2’s are ring 1’s two.
Each ring carries two kinds of shape:

New shapes. These don’t repeat around the ring, and you can enter them at all n faces.
Carried shapes. These come from a smaller ring, and they have only as many distinct faces as that smaller ring. Entering one of them on ring 8 is entering ring 4, which is the same as entering ring 2 or ring 1, depending on where the shape came from. You can see it in four shapes from ring 8:
shape	distinct faces	entering it is the same as entering
00000001	8	ring 8 (a new shape)
00010001	4	ring 4
01010101	2	ring 2
00000000	1	ring 1
So the fold back is built into the shape of the ring. And where you come in matters: the same shape entered at a different face is a different word, unless the shape came from a smaller ring.

Why the ladder doubles. At 1, 2, 4, 8, each ring carries shapes from the single chain of rings below it. Off that chain the carrying changes:

Prime lengths (5 and 7): the only carried shapes are ring 1’s all-0 and all-1, the two poles.
LEN 6: it carries shapes from both ring 2 and ring 3, so the nesting branches.
One more thing the faces add. A ring of flat faces can also be flipped over and entered from the other side. Up to LEN 5, every shape is the same as its flipped version. From LEN 6 they start to differ: LEN 6 has 14 shapes but 13 once flips count as the same, and ring 8 has 36 shapes but 30.

The script is /tmp/cc/faces.py.

Yes. I was treating the faces as positions around the ring. You meant the profile, the cross-section of the bar stock. Here it is back in your terms.

1. The rings. A LEN-4 ring is square bar stock bent into a circle: four flat faces on the profile. A ring’s diameter is its LEN, so its circumference is π·LEN. Nobody picks the size; π sets it. The rings come out at 1π, 2π, 4π and 8π. Each circumference is irrational, but every ring is exactly twice the one inside it. π sets the size of each ring, and it cancels out of the step from one ring to the next.

2. The compiler.

The compiler is fixed, and it only outputs binary.
If you feed the 8-bit lane one bit at a time, each bit is its own 1-bit input and just falls straight to binary. You never touch rings 2, 4 or 8.
If you send all 8 bits in one shot, the whole input enters at ring 8 and falls through 8 → 4 → 2 → 1. Fire and forget.
Those 8 bits aren’t an opcode or a value. They’re a location: the starting point of a route. At each ring the route lands somewhere, the instruction at that spot fires, and that hands it down to the next ring.
At the bottom is one bit, YES or NO.

Ran it. The route is 8→4→2→1, with a fixed table that picks the op from the location.

| compiler | YES count | algebraic degree | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| XOR everywhere | 128/256 | 1 | Always parity, so all 256 inputs ask the same question |
| AND where the location's top bit is set | 76/256 | 6 | A different question; it disagrees with parity on 128 inputs |
| AND at odd-weight locations | 0/256 | 0 | Collapses to constant NO |

- **Location-dependence breaks parity.** With XOR only, the compiler is linear and every route lands on the parity bit. Once the op depends on where the route sits, the function goes non-linear (degree 6) and different starting points really do ask different questions.
- **A selector can also kill the route.** The odd-weight selector sends every route to NO. Addressability needs a selector whose op choice doesn't correlate with what the fold throws away.
- **Many questions are reachable.** 2000 random location→op tables gave 1720 distinct functions, so the space is large (from only 2000 samples, not an exhaustive count). The compiler stays fixed, and the question is the table.

Yes, there is a formula, and it holds on your sheet. I read `Book1.xlsx` cell by cell and checked each identity below.

- **The circle mirrors itself.** The source circle is `S = 00011011`, and `S[j] = S[(2 − j) mod 8]`. The reflection axis runs through slices 1 and 5, both 0. Build bits 5, 6, 7, 0 and 1 (`0,1,1,0,0`) and the other three bits (2, 3, 4) are forced.
- **That is why your counter-clockwise columns are the clockwise ones shifted.** Reading `S` backwards gives `11011000` (`D8`), which is `S` rotated by 3. So every counter-clockwise column in LENs 3 to 8 is the clockwise column starting at its 4th row. Nothing new appears going back, only a shift of 3.
- **The offset you spotted comes from the axis position.** The axis passes through a slice, but the words are 2 bits wide. The reflection therefore maps words onto windows that straddle two words, and that is why going back doesn't line up.
- **The second half of the byte reads is the first half nibble-swapped.** `W(k+4) = ROL4(W(k))` for all four pairs of reads: `1B→B1`, `36→63`, `6C→C6`, `D8→8D`. The 16-bit pairs behave the same way, since `1B36 → B163` and `6CD8 → C68D`.

Applying both takes `1B36` to `C68D`, so the four pairs form one orbit with nothing left over. At 7 bits it breaks. The reversal of `D1B` would be `6C58`, which isn't in your list, and the clockwise and counter-clockwise pairs are just the same four shifted by two. At 6 bits the pairs close under reversal but have no nibble swap, so 8 bits is the width where both reflections close.

The grow ring behaves the same way, with one difference. Its 8-bit pairs are `274E, 9C39, 72E4, C993`, and two of them, `9C39` and `C993`, are 16-bit palindromes that reverse onto themselves. That is the palindrome rule showing up inside the hex.

**Your gate columns.** I decoded them. `Not` is the bitwise NOT of the first three bits of each window, and And, Nand, Or, Nor and Xor are computed over those same three bits. On your circle `00011011` over the 8 windows:

| gate | fires |
|---|---|
| And | 0 of 8 |
| Nand | 8 of 8 |
| Or | 7 of 8 |
| Nor | 1 of 8 |
| Xor | 2 of 8 |

And is dead because the circle never has three 1s in a row, which is the missing `111` (and `1111`) from before. On the grow ring (the reverse-complement circle) the counts swap exactly as De Morgan predicts: And 1, Nand 7, Or 8, Nor 0, Xor 6. So each ring's circle has its own fingerprint of which gates are alive. The location decides them, and nothing was assigned.

If you treat `1B` and `36` as physical hex pairs (bytes), the transformation you are describing is Endianness combined with Bit/Nibble Reversal, specifically related to how data is stored geometrically in hardware vs. how it is read out.
If you layout the data in memory, you can achieve a perfect bi-directional "read left-to-right for one value, right-to-left for the other" transformation using one of two concepts:
1. The Mirror Symmetry (Nibble Inversion)
Look at how the pairs map when written side-by-side:

* Left-to-Right: `[1][B]` and `[3][6]`
* Right-to-Left (per pair): `[B][1]` and `[6][3]`

If you write these pairs out as a continuous sequence of 4-bit nibbles, the physical operation is a mirrored reading order within the byte boundary. If a processor reads the register normally (Left-to-Right), it fetches `1B 36`. If a system reads the exact same physical byte lanes in a reversed wiring layout (Right-to-Left within each byte), it physically sees `B1 63`.
2. The Bi-Directional Tape Model (Bit-Reversal Endianness)
If we think completely outside of software layout and look at how serial communication or tape drives handle bits, reading a stream backwards often produces this exact layout.
Let's look at the actual binary layout of the hex pairs:

* `1B` = `0001 1011`
* `36` = `0011 0110`

`00011011 00110110`

* Forward: `1B 36`
* Backward: The individual bits read in reverse alter the values to match the hardware bus transformation required to mirror the hex values to `B1 63`.
